message.content:
**Freezing point of pure liquid water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Approximate freezing point |
|----------|----------------------------|
| **10 kPa** | **≈ 0 °C (273.15 K)** |

---

### Why it’s almost unchanged

* **Phase‑diagram background:**  
  In the water–ice system the solid–liquid equilibrium line runs nearly horizontal over the range of pressures encountered in everyday life (from the triple point at 0.61 kPa up through several hundred kilopascals).  

* **Clausius–Clapeyron estimate:**  
  \[
  \frac{dT}{dp}\;\approx\;-\,\frac{\Delta H_{\text{fus}}}{T_m\,V_{m,\text{liq}}\!-\!V_{m,\text{solid}}}
  \]
  Using standard values (\(\Delta H_{\text{fus}}\!\approx\!6.01\times10^3~\mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}},\;
   V_{m,\text{liq}}\!=0.00100~\mathrm{m^{3}\,kg^{-1}},\;
   V_{m,\text{solid}}\!=0.00109~\mathrm{m^{3}\,kg^{-1}}\)) yields  
  \(dT/dp \approx -7.5\times10^{-3}\ {\rm K\,MPa^{-1}}\).

  From ambient pressure (101.3 kPa) down to 10 kPa:
  \[
  \Delta p = 91.3\ \text{kPa}=0.0913\ \text{MPa}\\[4pt]
  \Delta T \approx dT/dp \times \Delta p 
            \approx (-7.5\times10^{-3})(0.0913)
            \approx -0.00068\ ^\circ\text{C}.
  \]

  Thus the shift is far smaller than one millikelvin—well within experimental uncertainty.

* **Practical implication:**  
  Even under reduced pressure such as 10 kPa, you would still observe ice forming only when the temperature drops *below* roughly 0 °C. There isn’t a noticeable “new” freezing point at this modestly lowered pressure.

---

#### Bottom line

At 10 kPa the freezing point of pure water remains effectively **0 °C (273.15 K)** – any measurable change is well below 0.01 °C and therefore practically insignificant.
